generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, reflective practice is not an optional study habit; it is how practitioners in the field keep developing. Sport scientists, coaches, therapists and sport managers are all expected to examine their own practice and act on what they find. The subjects differ in their evidence: a sport scientist weighs lab data and testing protocols, a coach weighs what happened in a session, a sport manager weighs participation figures. The shared point is development: looking back critically at a session, a decision or an analysis, judging it against the standards of the discipline, and changing what you do. Reflection is the evaluation phase of a practitioner's own self-regulation.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport and exercise science students reflecting on the same laboratory session that did not go to plan, a VO2 max test on an athlete that produced unreliable data.

Tom writes the session up because the module logbook requires it. His account sets out what happened, in order, and notes that he felt rushed but that the test finished and some numbers were recorded. It is honest and complete, but Tom treats reflection as a task to discharge. He does not ask why the data came out unreliable, weighs nothing against the testing protocol he was trained to follow, and changes nothing as a result. For Tom, reflection is compliance.

Amara writes the same session up as a scientist examining her own practice. She asks why the calibration drifted, weighs her choices against the protocol and good laboratory practice, and traces the unreliable data to her rushed setup rather than the athlete. She reaches a specific conclusion, to run a full calibration and checklist before the next test, and commits to it. For Amara, the session becomes development.

Both students reflected. Only Amara treated reflection as professional practice, using it to understand herself and improve.
generatedProse.summary: Across the School of Sport, reflective practice is the engine of a practitioner's self-regulated development. It is the evaluation phase in which you look back critically at your own practice against the standards of your discipline, and keep doing so across a career in training, clinic, laboratory and management. You can now articulate why it matters, appraise how well a practitioner reflects, and judge what owning it demands of you. The next lesson gives you Kolb's cycle as a structure for reflecting critically on a single experience.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection professional practice rather than compliance?

items.text: She weighed her own choices against the testing protocol and good laboratory practice, and committed to a specific change.
She produced a longer and more detailed account of the laboratory session.
She completed the module logbook entry on time.
She described exactly what happened in the session, in order.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing her practice against the discipline's standards and committing to a change is reflection as development.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did beyond recording the session.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's reflection was professional practice because she weighed her choices against the testing protocol and committed to a change, not because it was longer, on time or well ordered.
